title: Opening Up Kernel-Bypass TCP Stacks
problem: Kernel-bypass TCP stacks with different design choices for throughput and latency have never been systematically compared across representative workloads, making it difficult to understand performance trade-offs when handling both bulk data transfers over multi-hundred gigabit Ethernet and small request-response messages requiring low latency.
motivation: Understanding performance characteristics and design trade-offs of different kernel-bypass TCP stacks is essential for developing practical network stacks that can efficiently support modern datacenter applications.
method: The researchers compared six different TCP network stacks—both kernel-bypass versions (which skip the operating system for faster data sending) and traditional in-kernel ones—by running them on representative workloads: bulk data transfers over multi-hundred gigabit Ethernet and small request-response messages. They measured throughput (how much data flows per second) and latency (response time) to understand which design choices work best for each workload type.
key_novelty: This is the first systematic comparison of kernel-bypass TCP stacks across representative workloads, showing that no single design excels at both bulk data transfers and low-latency request handling.
contributions: Comprehensive benchmark suite comparing six kernel-bypass and in-kernel TCP stacks
Performance evaluation across bulk transfer and request-response workloads
Analysis demonstrating that existing stacks cannot efficiently handle different workload types simultaneously
Discussion of design pathways toward practical kernel-bypass stack implementations
primary_theme: Comparative performance analysis of kernel-bypass network stacks
